blocks.text: A surgical drain is a tube or device inserted into a wound, body cavity or operative site to remove accumulated fluid, blood, pus, air or other unwanted material.
It helps prevent fluid accumulation, permits monitoring of postoperative drainage and, in selected circumstances, reduces the risk of complications associated with collections.
Surgical drains are commonly used following abdominal surgery, breast surgery, orthopaedic procedures, thoracic surgery and the drainage of selected abscesses.
OSCE identification statement:

“This is a surgical drain, used to evacuate fluid, blood, pus or air from a surgical site or body cavity. It may be an open or closed system and may function by gravity, capillary action or suction, depending on its design.”
The components depend on the type of drain presented. A closed suction drain typically contains the following:

blocks.text: Exam tip: A Penrose drain does not normally have a suction bulb or closed collection reservoir. Always label only the components present on the instrument shown.

items.text: Material: Commonly silicone, latex rubber or another medical-grade polymer.
Flexibility: Must conform to the operative site without kinking excessively.
Drainage openings: May include fenestrations to facilitate fluid entry.
Diameter: Selected according to the anticipated fluid, viscosity and site.
Length: Depends on the surgical field and the required route.
Collection method: Open drainage, gravity drainage or closed suction.
Sterility: Supplied sterile or prepared according to the intended clinical use.
Radiopacity: Some drains contain radiopaque material to facilitate identification on imaging.
Fixation: Many drains require sutures or another securement method.

blocks.text: Surgical drains are classified according to their mechanism and whether the drainage system is open or closed.
1. Passive drains
Drainage occurs through gravity, capillary action or pressure gradients.
Example: Penrose drain.
Uses: Selected superficial wounds, cavities or abscess drainage where an open system is appropriate.
2. Active drains
Negative pressure or suction helps draw fluid into a collection reservoir.
Examples: Jackson-Pratt (JP) drain and Redivac drain.
Uses: Selected postoperative wounds where controlled closed drainage is indicated.

items.text: Open drain: Fluid exits into a dressing or external collection arrangement; contamination risk may be greater.
Closed drain: Fluid passes through sealed tubing into a collection reservoir.
Closed suction drain: A closed system that uses negative pressure to facilitate drainage.
Gravity drain: Uses gravity to direct fluid into an appropriate collection system.

Flexible perforated tube drains.

blocks.text: A. Penrose drain
Passive, open drain
A soft, flexible tube that allows fluid to escape onto a dressing or into an appropriate external collection arrangement.

items.text: Simple and inexpensive.
Does not require a suction reservoir.
Can permit ascending contamination.
Requires careful dressing and skin care.

blocks.text: B. Jackson-Pratt (JP) drain
Closed suction drain
A flexible perforated tube connected to a compressible bulb reservoir.

items.text: The compressed bulb creates negative pressure.
Commonly used following breast, abdominal and selected reconstructive procedures.
Allows measurement of the drainage volume.
Requires maintenance of the suction system.

blocks.text: C. Redivac drain
Closed suction drain
Uses a vacuum reservoir to provide negative pressure.

items.text: Commonly used in selected orthopaedic and general surgical procedures.
Collects fluid in a closed reservoir.
Requires monitoring of output and suction function.

blocks.text: D. Corrugated drain
Usually passive
A flexible drain with a corrugated structure that facilitates drainage.

items.text: Used in selected wounds or cavities.
Does not usually require a suction reservoir.
May be associated with external contamination and dressing requirements.

blocks.text: E. Chest drain
Thoracic drainage system
A tube inserted into the pleural space and connected to an appropriate drainage system.

items.text: Used for pneumothorax, haemothorax and selected pleural effusions.
May use an underwater seal and/or regulated suction.
Requires specific monitoring for air leaks, fluid output and respiratory complications.

blocks.text: Important distinction: A chest drain is a specialised drainage system. Its underwater seal and pleural pressure requirements differ from those of a routine wound drain.
The drain's purpose is to provide a controlled route for unwanted material to leave a wound or body cavity.

items.text: Gravity: Fluid flows towards a lower collection point.
Capillary action: Fluid moves along narrow spaces or material.
Pressure gradients: Fluid moves from a higher-pressure area towards a lower-pressure area.
Negative pressure: Suction assists the movement of fluid into the drain.

blocks.text: A drain only works effectively when it is appropriately positioned, patent and connected to a functioning collection system.

blocks.title: Surgical drains may be used to:

items.text: Remove blood or serous fluid accumulating after surgery.
Drain pus from selected infected cavities or abscesses.
Reduce fluid accumulation in selected operative spaces.
Monitor postoperative bleeding or fluid production.
Drain the pleural space of air or fluid using a chest drain.
Facilitate drainage following selected breast, abdominal, plastic or orthopaedic procedures.
Manage selected postoperative collections under surgical or image-guided care.

rows: Selected abdominal operations or abscess drainage
Pleural drainage using a chest tube
Selected intracranial or spinal drainage systems designed for that purpose

blocks.text: High-yield point: Drains are not required after every operation. Their use should be based on the procedure, expected collection, clinical indication and evidence-based practice.

items.text: Facilitates removal of fluid, blood or pus.
Allows postoperative output to be monitored.
May help identify abnormal bleeding or changes in fluid production.
Closed systems reduce environmental contamination compared with open systems.
Suction drains can help evacuate fluid from selected spaces.
Some drains can be managed outside hospital when appropriate.
Specialised drains can manage air and fluid in body cavities.

Can cause pain or discomfort.

May cause skin irritation or pressure injury.
Can prolong wound care and require additional monitoring.
A drain can create a route for organisms to enter the wound.
Unnecessary drains may increase morbidity without improving outcomes.

blocks.text: 1. Infection
Organisms may enter through the drain tract or contaminated connections, particularly with prolonged use or poor drain care.
2. Bleeding
Insertion or movement of a drain may injure vessels. Fresh blood or a sudden increase in bloody output requires assessment.
3. Blockage or kinking
Clots, thick fluid, debris or compression can prevent drainage and lead to fluid accumulation.
4. Displacement or accidental removal
The drain may no longer reach the intended collection site, reducing effectiveness or injuring tissue.
5. Pain, tissue injury or pressure damage
Drains may irritate adjacent tissue, cause discomfort or contribute to pressure-related injury.
6. Retained drain fragment
Rarely, a drain may break during removal, requiring assessment and sometimes further intervention.
There are few universal contraindications because drain selection depends on the clinical problem.

items.text: Avoiding unnecessary drain insertion.
Assessing bleeding risk and nearby anatomical structures.
Selecting an appropriate drain type and diameter.
Avoiding inappropriate placement through contaminated or vulnerable structures.
Ensuring that the collection system is suitable for the material being drained.
Securing the drain and documenting its insertion site and depth when relevant.

blocks.text: A drain should not be inserted blindly into a body cavity when safe placement cannot be assured.
This is a frequent OSCE topic.

items.text: The insertion site for redness, swelling, leakage and discharge.
The drain tubing for kinks, compression or visible blockage.
The collection reservoir for correct connections and function.
The fluid's colour, consistency and odour.
The total output and changes over time.

content_groups.group_title: C. Maintaining a closed suction drain

blocks.title: For a JP or similar drain:

items.text: Keep the reservoir and connections intact.
Maintain suction according to the manufacturer's instructions.
Empty and measure the contents using the prescribed aseptic technique.
Re-establish suction when required by the device design.
Record output and assess the insertion site.

blocks.text: Do not routinely irrigate, strip or milk a drain unless this is specifically indicated and authorised by the relevant clinical protocol.
Removal depends on the operation, drain type, clinical findings and output trend. There is no single output threshold suitable for every drain.
Removal should be performed by an appropriately trained clinician using the relevant protocol. If resistance, severe pain or suspected breakage occurs, stop and reassess rather than applying force.

blocks.text: Q1. Identify this instrument.
This is a surgical drain, used to remove unwanted fluid, blood, pus or air from an operative site or body cavity.
Q2. Classify surgical drains.
They may be classified as open or closed, passive or active, and by their construction and intended anatomical site.
Q3. What is the difference between a Penrose and a JP drain?
A Penrose is typically an open passive drain; a JP is a closed suction drain with a compressible bulb reservoir.
Q4. What is the function of the fenestrations?
They allow fluid to enter the drain through openings along the portion positioned within the operative site.
Q5. What does sudden fresh blood in a drain suggest?
It may indicate postoperative bleeding and requires prompt assessment, particularly if output is increasing or the patient is unstable.
Q6. Why might a drain stop producing fluid?
The cavity may have stopped producing fluid, or the drain may be blocked, kinked, displaced or malfunctioning.
Q7. Name four complications of surgical drains.
Infection, bleeding, blockage, displacement, pain and tissue injury are important examples.
Q8. Are drains necessary after every operation?
No. They should be used when clinically indicated because unnecessary drainage can cause complications without providing benefit.
Q9. What is the purpose of a chest drain's underwater seal?
It allows air and fluid to leave the pleural space while helping prevent air from flowing back into it.

items.text: Identify the drain and state its purpose.
Label the tubing, fenestrations, connectors and reservoir where present.
Distinguish passive from suction drains.
Distinguish open from closed systems.
Give examples of Penrose, JP, Redivac and chest drains.
List indications, advantages, disadvantages and complications.
Interpret common changes in drainage output.
Describe drain care and the principles of safe removal.
Penrose: Open, passive drain.
Jackson-Pratt: Closed suction drain with a bulb.
Redivac: Closed suction drain with a vacuum reservoir.
Chest drain: Specialised pleural drainage system.
Safety rule: Sudden fresh bleeding, loss of function with clinical deterioration, or signs of distal or adjacent tissue compromise require prompt assessment.
